title: Time to Build
sum: On the first day of the sixth month of Darius's second year (29 August 520 BC), the word of the LORD comes through Haggai to the governor Zerubbabel and the high priest Joshua. The people have been saying that the time has not come to rebuild the Temple. Haggai answers with questions and a pattern: they live in finished houses while God's house lies desolate, they sow much and harvest little, and the drought is the LORD's doing. He says twice, "Take your ways to heart," and asks for wood from the hills.

This time the leaders listen. The rest of the remnant listens with them, the LORD sends the short promise "I am with you," and he rouses the spirit of the governor, the high priest and the people. Twenty-three days after the first message, on 21 September, they come and begin the work. The chapter is one speech, one answer, and one start.
readings: The failed harvests are the old curses of Deuteronomy 28 and Leviticus 26. The prophet does not invent a new rule: he reads what is happening through what the covenant already said, and offers the people a way out in the same terms (build, and the LORD will be pleased).
Read as a call to leaders

The first audience is two men, the governor and the high priest. The people respond only after their leaders do (1:12), and the LORD's "stirring" falls on the leaders first (1:14). It is a story about how a stalled community gets moving.
Read as a warning about misuse
Because 1:6-11 links lean harvests with an unbuilt house, it is often quoted as a promise of wealth for giving. The Hebrew speaks to one province in one year; see the note at 1:9.

views.H: The setting is Judah as a small Persian province in 520 BC, eighteen years after Cyrus's decree (Ezra 1:1-4) and in the unsettled years when Darius I put down revolts. The work on the Temple, begun under Cyrus, had stopped (Ezra 4:24). The drought and poor harvests are real events in these years (1:6, 10-11). By the usual conversion the dates fall on 29 August (1:1) and 21 September (1:15).
views.C: The book speaks of Haggai in the third person and gives its dates in a set formula, so it was shaped by an editor, in Haggai's circle or soon after (Wolff, Meyers and Meyers, Petersen, Kessler). Many see the account of the response (1:12-14) as the editor's narrative frame around the oracle. The wordplay on "desolate" and "drought" (1:4, 9, 11) is one reason the prophetic speech is thought to be carefully composed. The Greek puts the date of 1:15 at the start of chapter 2.
views.J: Jewish readers have used the book for the Second Temple's story. The Talmud ties the missing letter in "I will be honored" (1:8) to the five things the Second Temple lacked (Yoma 21b) and counts Haggai among the last prophets, after whom the Holy Spirit left Israel (Yoma 9b). Haggai, Zechariah and Malachi are also named as the sources of the Aramaic Targum of the Prophets (Megillah 3a). Rashi's comment on 1:8 draws the lesson from the spelling. Rashi on 1:2 says the people thought God would not keep his word, since their enemies had stopped the work the first time.
views.X: Christian commentators have read the unbuilt house as the church (the people are the temple: 1 Corinthians 3:16; 1 Peter 2:5) or as the believer's own heart, and applied 1:4-9 to people who look after their own comfort before God's work (Jerome's and Calvin's commentaries on the Twelve). The misuse of 1:6-11 as a promise of wealth for giving is a modern reception, and the Hebrew does not support it.

deep.b: Haggai gives six dates, which fall on four different days, and they run in order. By the usual conversion: 1:1, first day of the sixth month, 29 August 520 BC; 1:15, twenty-fourth day of the sixth month, 21 September 520; 2:1, twenty-first day of the seventh month, 17 October 520; 2:10, 2:18 and 2:20, twenty-fourth day of the ninth month, 18 December 520. The whole book therefore covers a little under four months. The first date is the new moon, a festival day (Numbers 28:11-15), when people were free to gather; the second is the start of the work; the third is the seventh day of Booths; and the last three share one day. The Temple was finished on the third of Adar in Darius's sixth year (Ezra 6:15), about 12 March 515 BC.
deep.refs: Haggai 1:1; Haggai 1:15; Haggai 2:1; Haggai 2:10; Haggai 2:18; Haggai 2:20; Ezra 6:15; Numbers 28:11-15

deep.b: Ezra tells it in two stages. After Cyrus's decree, Zerubbabel and Jeshua built the altar and laid the Temple's foundation (Ezra 3), but local opposition frightened the builders (Ezra 4:4-5) and the work "stayed stopped until the second year of the reign of Darius king of Persia" (Ezra 4:24). Haggai says nothing of the opposition. His diagnosis is that the people put their own houses first. Scholars weigh the two: opposition and poverty as real causes, and the excuse of the seventy years as the reason the people gave. Bedford has argued that little or no building happened before 520 at all, and that Ezra 3 reads the first return in the light of the second; this is a minority view.

echoes: Ezra 4:24; Ezra 5:1-2; Ezra 6:14-15; Deuteronomy 28:38-40; Deuteronomy 11:13-17; Amos 4:6-9; Isaiah 6:9; Exodus 3:12; Joshua 1:9; Zechariah 1:1-6; Zechariah 8:9-12

settings.what: The call to build the house
settings.by: The LORD of Armies, through Haggai the prophet
settings.to: Zerubbabel the governor of Judah and Joshua the high priest, and through them "this people" of the province of Judah
settings.when: 29 August 520 BC (the first day of the sixth month, the new moon), the second year of Darius, eighteen years after Cyrus's decree and during the stoppage of the Temple work
settings.why: To turn an excuse ("the time has not come") into action. The speech asks the leaders to look at what has been happening: lean harvests, a drought, houses finished while the house of God is not. It ties the hardship to the unbuilt Temple in the language of the covenant curses (Deuteronomy 28), and ends with a command small enough to do: go up, bring wood, build. Knowing the audience (a poor province, a recent political crisis, an unfinished Temple) makes the speech a call to priorities, not a general rule about giving.
views: The text names only the governor and the high priest as addressees, and the people hear the message through them (1:12).
A message at the New Moon assembly
Some commentators picture the prophet speaking at the new moon gathering, when people were free from work (Numbers 28:11-15). The text does not say where it was spoken.

settings.what: The people obey and the work begins
settings.by: The narrator (an editor), reporting Haggai's short word and the LORD's rousing
settings.to: The reader, with Haggai's "I am with you" given to "the people"
settings.when: Between 29 August and 21 September 520 BC, with the work beginning on the twenty-fourth day of the sixth month
settings.why: To record the first result of the prophet's word and to give the promise that follows obedience. The book's own first readers, a later Judean community, are meant to see that the building began with a small obedience and a short promise, not with a finished plan.
settings.readers: For the readers of the Persian period and after, who knew the finished Temple, this paragraph says how it started: a listening leadership, a roused spirit, and the sentence "I am with you."

title: The Last Glory
sum: Four weeks later, on the seventh day of the feast of Booths (17 October 520), the word comes again, this time to the leaders and the remnant. The old people remember the first Temple, and the new one looks like nothing. The LORD answers: be strong, work, I am with you, my spirit is standing among you. In a little while he will shake the heavens, the earth and the nations; the prized things of the nations will come; the last glory of this house will be greater than the first, and in this place he will give peace.

On 18 December the prophet asks the priests two questions about holy meat and an unclean touch, and says that this people, and its offerings, are unclean while the Temple lies unbuilt. He asks them to look back at the failed harvests and promises blessing from that day. The same day, a second word comes to Zerubbabel alone: the LORD will shake the heavens, overturn the thrones of the nations, and make him like a seal ring, his chosen servant.
readings: Read as encouragement for a small beginning

The three messages answer discouragement, uncertainty and fear. They grant the sense of loss (2:3), promise the LORD's presence (2:4-5), tie the future to the LORD's power over the nations (2:6-9, 21-23), and offer a date after which things change (2:15-19).
Read as a prophecy of Christ and the church

Christian readers have found in the shaking and the last glory the coming of Christ, the church as the true temple, or the end of the age (Hebrews 12:26-27). The Hebrew of 2:7 supports a collective sense, and the person of Christ is a reception, not a translation (see the card).
Read as a hope that was not fulfilled in its own terms

Critical readers note that Zerubbabel never became king, that the Persian Empire was not overturned in Haggai's lifetime, and that the later Jewish debate whether the Second Temple's glory was greater shows the promise was not obviously kept.

views.H: In October 520 the Persian world was still unsettled by Darius's first years, and Haggai's "shaking" fits those events or a hope for more. The Temple was completed by March 515 BC (Ezra 6:15). The date of 18 December falls in the rainy season, three months after work began; the "failed harvests" of 2:16-17 are those of the years before. Zerubbabel disappears from the record after the work begins.
views.C: Scholars treat 2:10-19 as the hardest passage: the referent of "this people" (Judeans, Samaritans, or the whole land), the meaning of "from this day on back" and of "the day the foundation was laid," and the order of the dates. The Greek has long additions at 2:9 and 2:14. The "desire of all nations" is read as a collective, not a person, by most critics.
views.J: Jewish tradition asks how far the promise of "greater" glory was kept. Rashi on 2:9 reports that Rav and Samuel disagreed about what "greater" means, one saying the building and the other the years (410 for the first house, 420 for the second). The Talmud lists what the Second Temple lacked (Yoma 21b). Radak takes the "desire of all nations" (2:7) as the nations' valuables brought to the Temple. Rashi on 2:22 says the Persian kingdom would fall to another, and on 2:23 takes the seal ring as Zerubbabel himself, born to Jeconiah after his repentance.
views.X: Christians have read 2:6-9 of Christ: the Vulgate's "Desired of all nations," the Advent hymn "Dear desire of every nation," Hebrews 12:26-27 on the shaking, the church as God's temple (1 Corinthians 3:16; Ephesians 2:20-22). Zerubbabel, a named ancestor of Jesus (Matthew 1:12-13; Luke 3:27), is read as a type of Christ in the Fathers and Calvin. These are receptions; the cards show where the churches differ.
views.F: Some read 2:6-9 and 2:21-23 as still to come: a final shaking of the world, the nations bringing their treasure to a restored temple, and a Davidic ruler like a seal ring. Dispensationalist readings join them to Ezekiel 40-48 and the millennial kingdom; others join them to the new creation (Hebrews 12:26-28; Revelation 21). Haggai himself gives no date.

deep.h: Holy and unclean: what the priests said
deep.b: The two questions of 2:12-13 are a lesson in how holiness and uncleanness behave. Holy meat carried in a robe does not make bread or oil holy by touch. A person made unclean by a dead body does make what he touches unclean. The prophet then says, "So it is with this people." The comparison is that holiness does not spread by contact (their sacrifices and their altar, offered while the Temple lay unbuilt, do not sanctify their work), and uncleanness does (their neglect taints everything they handle). The Greek expands the verse with a charge of corrupt gain.

deep.h: The seal ring, and a grandson
deep.b: Jeremiah had said that if King Jehoiachin (Coniah) were a seal ring on the LORD's right hand, the LORD would pull him off and give him to Nebuchadnezzar (Jeremiah 22:24-25). His descendants, Jeremiah added, would not sit on David's throne (Jeremiah 22:30). Haggai names Jehoiachin's grandson as the LORD's seal ring. He does not call him king. The shaking of 2:21-22 is the setting: the thrones of the nations fall, and the one the LORD has chosen is put on his hand. The promise stands on the last page of the book with no sequel. The New Testament genealogies place Zerubbabel in Jesus' ancestry (Matthew 1:12-13; Luke 3:27), and the church read the promise in that light.
deep.refs: Jeremiah 22:24-25; Jeremiah 22:30; Haggai 2:23; Matthew 1:12-13; Luke 3:27; 1 Chronicles 3:17-19

echoes: Hebrews 12:26-28; 1 Kings 8:10-11; Exodus 40:34-35; Ezekiel 43:1-5; Isaiah 60:5-11; Psalm 50:10; Joshua 1:6-9; Numbers 19:11-22; Leviticus 6:27; Amos 4:9; Zechariah 4:6-10; Zechariah 8:9-12; Jeremiah 22:24-25; Judges 7:22; Ezekiel 38:21; Sirach 49:11-12; Matthew 1:12-13; Luke 3:27; 1 Corinthians 3:16; 1 Peter 2:5

settings.what: "Be strong": the first glory and the last
settings.by: The LORD of Armies, through Haggai the prophet
settings.to: Zerubbabel the governor, Joshua the high priest and the remnant of the people, gathered in Jerusalem
settings.when: 17 October 520 BC, the twenty-first day of the seventh month, the seventh day of Booths, four weeks after the work began
settings.why: To meet discouragement. The old men who had seen Solomon's Temple wept when a foundation was laid (Ezra 3:12-13; whether that was in 538 or in the same work Haggai addresses is debated, see the note at Haggai 2:18), and the builders could see how little they had. The message names the grief ("Is it not like nothing in your eyes?"), calls for strength, promises the LORD's presence and his spirit, and says that the nations' wealth and a greater glory will come. It is not a prediction of a particular date; it is a reason to keep building.
views: A message for the festival crowd
The date falls on the seventh day of Booths, when pilgrims were in the city and Solomon's Temple had been dedicated at the same feast (1 Kings 8:2). Several commentators note the match.
The glory as the nations' treasure
The shaking brings the wealth of the nations to the house, as in Isaiah 60:5-11; the next verse speaks of silver and gold.
The glory as a person or the end of the age
Christian readers take the shaking and the glory as the coming of Christ or the end of the age; see the card below.

settings.what: A ruling on holy and unclean, and the turn to blessing
settings.by: Haggai the prophet, asking the priests for a ruling and then speaking the LORD's word
settings.to: The priests (for the ruling) and "this people" (for the application); the hearers of 2:15-19 are the same community that heard the first message
settings.when: 18 December 520 BC, the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month, three months after the work began
settings.why: To tell the community that its work and offerings are not yet clean because the Temple is not built, and then to say what changes: from the 24th, the day the LORD's temple "was founded" (2:18; what that day marks is debated), the LORD will bless. The priests' ruling gives the argument its authority; the failed harvests give it its evidence; the promise gives it a start date.
views: "This people" are the Judeans themselves, whose altar worship is incomplete without the Temple (Ackroyd, Meyers and Meyers, Petersen, Kessler).
Rothstein (1908) argued the oracle refers to the Samaritans; most scholars reject it.
A general judgment on the unbuilt Temple's effect on everything the people handle.

settings.what: The word to Zerubbabel: a seal ring
settings.by: The LORD of Armies, through Haggai the prophet
settings.to: Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, governor of Judah, alone
settings.when: 18 December 520 BC, a second word on the same day as 2:10-19
settings.why: To tell the governor, a grandson of the Davidic king whom the LORD had once pulled off like a seal ring (Jeremiah 22:24), that the LORD's shaking of the nations will end with him chosen. It is an assurance for a man doing a risky job under foreign rule; it is not a call to revolt, and the LORD, not Zerubbabel, does the overturning.
views: A promise to the Davidic governor of his day, never carried out in the sources (many critical readers).
The Fathers and Reformers read Zerubbabel as a figure of Christ; see the card.
A promise for the end of the age
Zerubbabel's line is kept for a coming Davidic king (Dispensationalist readings, which set the shaking at the end of the age).
Rashi takes the seal ring as Zerubbabel himself: Jeconiah's repentance undid the decree that he would be childless, and Zerubbabel was born to him and made as a signet (Rashi on 2:23).

traditions.q: Is the desire of all nations (Haggai 2:7) Christ, or the nations' treasures?
views: The Latin Vulgate reads "the Desired of all nations will come," and the Latin church read it of Christ, as the Fathers did; the Advent antiphon "O King of the nations, and their desire" echoes it. Many modern Catholic scholars and translations read the Hebrew plural, "the treasures of the nations," without denying the Christological use.

The Greek-speaking church read the Septuagint's "the chosen things of all the nations will come" of the nations that come to Christ and his church, and of Christ's own coming; its Fathers (Cyril of Alexandria, Theodoret of Cyrus) comment on the Greek, not the Hebrew. No modern Orthodox commentary or liturgical use is cited here.

Luther's German Bible renders the phrase "aller Heiden Trost" ("the comfort of all the nations"), at German 2:8, which is English 2:7, and he read the verse of Christ in his lectures on Haggai (1526); the Lutheran tradition has followed him.

Calvin held that the Hebrew verb is plural and that the phrase means "the desirable things" of the nations brought to God, rather than a title of Christ alone; he found the fulfillment in the gathering of the nations under Christ's kingdom.

John Gill read "the desire of all nations" as Christ, whom the Gentiles in their need desire, and the "house" filled with glory as the Temple in which Christ taught. Gill is one Particular Baptist commentator and does not speak for every Baptist.

The shaking and the filling of the house with glory belong to the future kingdom: Christ's return and a restored temple, as in Ezekiel 40-48. The "desire" is Christ at his second coming or the nations' wealth brought to that temple. No named Dispensationalist teacher is cited for this verse here; the summary is of the general pattern of that tradition and is unsourced.

traditions.q: Is Zerubbabel the "seal ring" (Haggai 2:23) a type of Christ, or a promise for his own day? (Orthodox, Lutheran and Baptist teachers are not cited on this verse; no different view is claimed for them.)
views: The Fathers read Zerubbabel as a figure of Christ, the true Davidic ruler and the one who builds God's house; Jerome in his commentary on Haggai treats the promise as fulfilled in the Savior. The Catechism teaches that the Old Testament is read in the light of Christ (Catechism 128-130).

Calvin took the promise to Zerubbabel as a pledge of the Davidic kingdom that would come in Christ: the governor stands for the line through which Christ was born (Matthew 1:12-13), and the shaking of the kingdoms is the overthrow of earthly powers by Christ.

The overthrow of the thrones of the nations (2:22) is a still-future event; the promise to the Davidic governor is kept in Christ's earthly reign at the end of this age, not in the church now. No named Dispensationalist teacher is cited for this verse here; the summary is of the general pattern of that tradition and is unsourced.
